outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Imaginary-Axis Projection of a Phasor
outline_section.learning_goal: Teach that the imaginary-axis projection of a phasor is its imaginary part, so a phasor of magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ projects to $A\sin\theta$ and a rotating phasor gives $x(t)=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Establish that the imaginary-axis projection of a phasor is its imaginary part, so a phasor with magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ has projection $A\sin\theta$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a unit phasor on the positive real axis, then move to a phasor of magnitude $A$ at a general angle $\theta$.
paragraph_plan: Connect this lesson to the previous phasor topics by stating that the tip of the phasor moves in the complex plane and that the imaginary-axis shadow is the sine-valued signal we want.
Begin with a fixed phasor and show that its imaginary-axis projection is the vertical component, so the projection equals $A\sin\theta$.
State the same rule in complex-number language by taking the imaginary part of $A e^{j\theta}$.
Replace the fixed angle with a time-dependent angle $\theta(t)=\omega t+\phi$ for counterclockwise rotation.
Summarize the bridge from phasor geometry to the time-domain sine and preview that later sections vary only magnitude, phase, and rotation direction.
